column2: Without knowing it, the Alberses get through the complexities of visas and paperwork with surprising ease: the Committee to Rescue German Artists, based in the United States, was helping them behind the scenes visas and administrative formalities Consequences: departure for Black Mountain College made possible

After a governance conflict at Rollins College (Florida), nine dismissed teachers come before an AAUP mediation panel, which clears them but cannot reinstate them; with sympathetic staff, they found a college with no autocratic chancellor and no board of trustees, with a flexible curriculum, aiming to educate the student as a person and as a citizen. Nine dismissed teachers; the grounds of a YMCA summer camp twenty miles from Asheville, on the edge of a small mountain town called Black Mountain. Consequences: The creation of an unaccredited college that becomes a major center of postwar art.
On his arrival, Albers declares: “I want to open eyes” — he wants to create an audience educated by his new perceptual strategies. Consequences: Albers's educational program defined

Just as the experimental test is taking root at Black Mountain, many European models of social and aesthetic experimental practice are being shut down by political persecution and by the “rappel à l'ordre,” the return to artistic tradition. Consequences: The Bauhaus project migrates to the United States and fragments

Shortly before Albers's arrival, the college's inaugural publication declares that the fine arts, often marginal in curricula, are there an integral part of the life of the college, of equal importance with the core subjects. Consequences: Places art at the heart of the educational project, justifying the recruitment of Albers.

A fatal accident involving the Dymaxion Car at the 1933 Chicago World's Fair leads automotive engineers to note that imitating aeronautical airflow encourages dangerous drifting on city roads Consequences: Adds to the file of Fuller's “dangerous” inventions

The Bauhaus moves to Berlin in 1933 under the direction of Mies van der Rohe and is closed shortly afterward under Nazi pressure. The Alberses, aged forty-five (Josef) and thirty-four (Anni), find themselves out of work, in an atmosphere increasingly hostile to abstract art. Josef 45, Anni 34 Consequences: Emigration to the United States

Johnson learns that Black Mountain College, newly founded and experimental, in North Carolina, is looking for an exceptional art teacher and suggests Josef. The college offers posts to both Alberses, who at first think North Carolina might be in the Philippines. They accept, warning that Josef does not speak English; the faculty urges them to come despite the language barrier. They sail for America in November 1933. the Philippines confusion; the warning “Josef spoke no English” Consequences: Arrival in New York, then settling at Black Mountain
Anni feels guilty because her heritage is one of the factors forcing Josef (a Catholic) and her to leave Germany.

The Alberses at once relish the dynamism and energy of New York, the eagerness of the crowds in the museums, the openness of the people at Black Mountain; they approve of a world in which their close new friends (BMC colleagues) went on their honeymoon with backpacks. Josef remains in part a nostalgic German; Anni feels completely at home in the United States, from the years when Roosevelt seemed a kindly uncle. colleagues' backpacking honeymoon

After emigrating to the United States with her husband Josef, Anni Albers establishes the weaving department and begins teaching in 1933; there she first puts into practice her method of playful productivity. Consequences: The first application of her material-based teaching outside the Bauhaus.

After the Nazis close the Bauhaus, Philip Johnson suggests that the Alberses come to the United States; interested in Josef's painting and teaching and struck by Anni's industrial textile work, he recommends them both for posts at the brand-new Black Mountain College in North Carolina. Consequences: The posts make immigration possible; they hold them until 1948. Their arrival is covered by the press, which also highlights Anni's achievements as a weaver and textile designer.

The closure of the Bauhaus in 1933 foreshadowed the war years and led some of the best European intellectuals and artists to consider a career in the United States — a context from which Black Mountain benefited. Consequences: The potential arrival of European artists, Josef Albers among them, at the college.

Early in 1933, Rice's public criticism of Rollins and its administration, together with his verbal attacks on certain teachers and students, leads to the termination of his contract. Consequences: Triggers an AAUP investigation, considerable national publicity, and the founding of Black Mountain College in September 1933.
Rice's dismissal from Rollins prompts an investigation by the American Association of University Professors and a highly publicized controversy.

Rice's public criticism of Rollins, its administration, and certain teachers and students leads to the termination of his contract in early 1933 Consequences: An AAUP investigation; an exodus of dissident teachers and students to Black Mountain

The AAUP, with Arthur Lovejoy at the head of its investigative arm, clears Rice and censures Rollins; by the time the report is published, Rice has already taken dissidents to Black Mountain Consequences: A highly publicized dispute over academic freedom
Only Lovejoy ventures to offer Rice positive advice: to look for a post in a larger institution, where he would be spread out more, diluted. the phrase “where you'd spread a little thinner”

Not much interested in the turmoil around Rice, Weston follows his girlfriend Nan Chapin, a determined supporter of Rice; Rice offers him a full scholarship on learning that his family could not pay for his studies. full scholarship Consequences: Weston becomes a Black Mountain student

Barbara Dreier will later exclaim that a college was created in six weeks; Ted Dreier adds: from nothing, without money, in the middle of the Depression. six weeks; no capital; the context of the Great Depression Consequences: the start of a start-up saga punctuated by small victories and setbacks
A meeting for planning and philosophical discussion lasts nearly a week at Josiah Spurr's summer house in Alstead, with former Rollins students and teachers. nearly a week of discussions

Nell regularly left with her daughter Mary for Sullivan, Indiana, sometimes encouraged (and given train fare) by her brother Frank, who liked to know someone was near their aging parents, sometimes driven by growing marital difficulties. Before Rice's final departure from Winter Park, they leave town, leaving Rice to stew alone over his dismissal. train ticket paid for by Nell's brother Frank

Rice and Dreier are looking for someone to head drawing and painting, the simplest thing: between you, the pencil, the paper, and your ability to see. Dreier's recommendations from the art world point to people suited to an art school, not to art education as conceived at Black Mountain. Rice explicitly refuses an art school. They also want someone manly, to counter the image of art as a “sissy subject” among the male students. Consequences: Margaret Lewisohn steers them toward Edward Warburg.

A few weeks after the agreement with Black Mountain, Albers receives an offer from Edwin Park, head of the art program at Bennington, who wanted to transplant the Bauhaus philosophy rather than let Albers teach in his own way. Albers was no doubt also glad to be already committed elsewhere. Consequences: Black Mountain got Albers by a narrow margin.

The daughter of Charles Templeman Loram, the Yale professor who founded the department of Race Relations; a Swarthmore graduate with honors in three years, with no prospects in 1932 at the bottom of the Depression, she obtains her master's degree from Columbia in the spring of 1933. Aydelotte puts her in touch with Rice, who interviews her briefly in New York (a neutral, polite interview, photos of the site). A few days later Dreier offers her the post; she accepts out of a taste for adventure, turning down the doctorate. As Wunsch has backed out, she must also teach drama, about which she admits knowing almost nothing. Consequences: She takes English and dramatics.

Joe Martin, a graduate of Haverford and Oxford, was beginning a doctorate at Columbia; tired of student life, he applies at the urging of his sister, a Rice supporter at Rollins. Two meetings with Rice, and he is hired for English.

During a midsummer session at the Aydelottes', Rice simply wants to announce the college and let students and donors flock in; Dreier, scandalized, considers this irresponsible without a budget. They go to bed still arguing; Dreier stays up all night drawing up a budget, presented at breakfast the next morning. Expenses: $30,000; income: $15,000 from fifteen students paying $1,000 each (several scholarships planned) and $15,000 from donors. Aydelotte advises them they had better make Ted treasurer — a post he will hold for sixteen years. $30,000 in expenses; 15 students × $1,000 Consequences: Dreier becomes treasurer for sixteen years.

Rice spends an afternoon on Naushon explaining the project to Malcolm Forbes, a colleague at Rollins who admired him grudgingly (too blunt, arrogant), and whom Rice had nonetheless defended when colleagues wanted to drive him out of Rollins. Forbes offers $5,000; his wife Ethel matches the sum as Rice is leaving. Later in the summer Forbes nearly backs out; Dreier persuades him and his wife to make good on their pledges, and Barbara and Ted Dreier see as much of the Forbeses socially as they can. Until Malcolm Forbes's death in 1941, only Rice and Dreier know the identity of these anonymous donors. $5,000 from Malcolm Forbes + $5,000 from Ethel Forbes Consequences: This gift makes the founding of the college financially possible; the year's other guarantors: Arthur S. Dwight, William Barstow, and Dreier's parents, Edward and Ethel Dreier ($2,000).
The Dreier couple gives two thousand dollars to the college project. 2000 dollars Consequences: Funding for the founding

The catalog, cautious so as to reassure paying parents, stresses proven methods and plays down the “experimental” label; it champions the arts and explains how teaching is organized. 1933-1934 catalog Consequences: Defines the college's public image
A 1932 Rollins graduate, Elizabeth Vogler holds the post of registrar and general administrative assistant.
Rice intercepts Hope Stephens as she goes out to meet a student he considers unworthy of her, draws her aside, and asks her whether she would want him to be the father of her children.
Nell Rice makes two trips to her family in Sullivan, Indiana, during the fall, while Rice stays on to preside over the college's beginnings. two trips

The Third Reich forces the Bauhaus to close; its members scatter: Klee to Switzerland, Kandinsky to Paris, others to America and Israel. Consequences: The diaspora of the Bauhäusler, the Alberses among them, to America.

After the school closes in 1933, the Bauhäusler flee to the United States. Albers begins teaching at the newly founded Black Mountain College in North Carolina and makes the Bauhaus principles of experimentation central to the education he advocates throughout the country. Consequences: The Vorkurs is passed on to BMC and then to Yale

To his parents' despair, Felix stays in Germany: he and Phroska are at the start of stage careers he does not want to give up, even though, to succeed in the German theater, he must denounce his father.

After fleeing Germany, Klee and Lily settle into an apartment that serves as studio, bedroom, and alcove kitchen, with a bathroom; they say they are glad to have hot water and central heating, well below their comfort at the Bauhaus. A view of the Alps; an alcove kitchen; hot water and central heating; Klee cooked his favorite recipes there Consequences: Klee, who had become a German citizen in Munich in his youth, cannot obtain Swiss citizenship
Lily describes their life in exile: they are like two happy children, and living with limitations makes one more aware of one's good fortune.

Scheyer hopes to get Solomon Guggenheim and his adviser Hilla Rebay (whom she nicknames “Rabbi”) to buy Kandinsky, but they are devoted exclusively to Rudolph Bauer, a mediocre abstractionist whose style vaguely imitates Kandinsky's. Scheyer's phrase: “Bauer is God and you are only a painter”. Consequences: America will not be the solution for Kandinsky.

A few months after their arrival in America, several of Albers's glass constructions arrive broken: American customs officers carelessly damaged them while taking them out of their meticulous packing. Albers keeps and repairs the fragments. Meticulous packing clumsily undone Consequences: Personal devastation; he nonetheless repairs and keeps them

A few months before Warburg's letter, Johnson runs into Anni in the street in Berlin and is invited to tea. Anni rightly sensed that the apartment, recently stripped down to the barest white and furnished with their works and the plainest chairs and tables, would intrigue him; she is also on the lookout for anything that might lead to a job for Josef. There Johnson discovers that some time earlier Lilly Reich, Mies van der Rohe's mistress, had shown him as her own fabric samples that were in fact Anni's. Johnson was also struck by the strength and serenity of Anni's textiles and by her subtle humor; Josef seemed to him too doctrinaire, and probably too homophobic. water was served there in pharmacist's flasks to avoid ornate carafes Consequences: Johnson will judge Anni the best textile designer he has ever met and will bring the Alberses over

Among other things, Holt reproaches Rice for having called a wood chisel one of the most beautiful objects in the world, for whispering in chapel, for having an indolent gait, for leaving fish scales in the sink of the college's beach cottage, and for wearing an athletic supporter on the beach. Two other teachers are dismissed shortly afterward; Ted Dreier, who taught physics, resigns in sympathy. Consequences: The group of outcasts at once founds Black Mountain with Rice at the helm

Alerted by Ethel Dreier to what the MoMA people were doing, Ted and Rice look at photos of the folded-paper experiments from Albers's preliminary course at the Bauhaus: it is exactly what they are looking for, all the more since they want to break the tradition that it is effeminate to be in the arts. Consequences: The decision to recruit Albers

A monument of rough bricks to Karl Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg (killed in 1919), adorned with the hammer and sickle on a five-pointed star; known only from photographs; destroyed by the Nazis rough bricks with jagged edges, abstract blocks

While Mies goes to Gestapo headquarters in Berlin every other day to learn the fate of the Bauhaus, he is pleased that Kandinsky has praised the house so highly to Galka Scheyer that he is asked to send photos to Hollywood; she plans to show them to an American collector who might want a similar home. Mies's trips to Gestapo headquarters every other day Consequences: Leads toward American migration

One morning, arriving by streetcar from Berlin and crossing the bridge from which the building can be seen, Mies finds the school surrounded by the Gestapo in black uniforms with bayonets. He runs; a sentry stops him; he invokes his status as tenant and goes in. The officer explains that they are investigating a case against the mayor of Dessau and are inspecting the founding documents of the Bauhaus. Mies summons everyone and orders everything opened for inspection, certain that there is nothing that could be construed against them. black uniforms, bayonets; streetcar, bridge; “Open everything for inspection” Consequences: The search lasts for hours; the agents, tired and hungry, call their headquarters, which orders them to close it and forget it.

Mies calls Rosenberg, the Nazi Party philosopher and head of the Bund Deutsche Culture, who can see him only at eleven at night. His friends Hilberseimer and Lilly Reich, fearing he will be killed, wait for him in a café across the street, behind the window, to see how he will come out. Mies and Rosenberg talk for an hour: Mies argues that the Bauhaus is a matter of technology, not politics; Rosenberg, a trained architect from Riga, rejects any rapprochement — the Bauhaus is supported by hostile forces, one army against another on the spiritual plane. He reproaches Mies for not changing the name when leaving Dessau and admits his hostility to the cantilever: “my feeling demands a support”. Mies, pointing to Rosenberg's shabby desk, which he says he would throw out of the window, sets out his ideal of objects one does not need to throw out of the window. an appointment at 11 p.m.; an hour's discussion; a café across the street Consequences: Rosenberg promises to see what he can do; Mies tells him not to delay.

Mies shows up at Gestapo headquarters every other day for exactly three months, convinced that he is within his rights: a private school, a signed contract, 27,000 marks committed. The waiting room has a bench barely four inches wide (about ten centimeters), designed to wear visitors out. He finally reaches the young head of the Gestapo, who says he is interested in the Bauhaus movement but is worried about Kandinsky; Mies vouches for him, and the officer warns that if anything happens, it is Mies who will be arrested. He promises to talk to Goering about it. every other day for 3 months; a bench 4 inches wide; a personal warning concerning Kandinsky Consequences: The school lives solely on the remaining money paid by Dessau.

At the opening of the House of German Art, Hitler gives the speech that sets Nazi cultural policy. Before that, nothing had been settled: Goebbels and Goering each had his own idea. After this speech, the Bauhaus is excluded. Consequences: All hope of a lasting official reopening collapses.

Mies finally receives the letter authorizing the reopening. He calls Lilly Reich and tells her to order champagne. She objects that they have no money; he insists. He gathers the faculty — Albers, Kandinsky, Hilberseimer, Peterhans — and announces the letter, then his proposal: to reply with thanks for the permission to reopen, but say the faculty has decided to close. Everyone accepts with delight, over the champagne ordered for this very moment. champagne despite the lack of money; the members present named Consequences: This, according to Mies, is the true end of the Bauhaus — known only to those who were there, Josef Albers among them.

Seven years after the Studebaker factory, he borrows welding equipment from a garage and begins the metal sculpture that will make him known. welding equipment borrowed from a garage Consequences: the birth of his work in direct metal
Smith makes his first piece of metal sculpture using sections of an old cart. sections of an old cart (wagon) as a “ready-made” Consequences: the start of his practice of recycled metal

Albers writes his name in the air, backward so that it can be read; no one understands, so he goes to the blackboard. Who saw it? To be honest: “Let's admit that we are visually underdeveloped”. Then everyone writes his name in the air, backward, upside down, in all four directions — eye and arm together. Words: “Let's admit that we are visually underdeveloped” Atmosphere: Theatrical play, surprise Stakes: Albers's first lesson in America

After studying English, Albers makes his first trip to the village alone, walks into a store, and greets the clerk with “Good-bye”. Words: “Good-bye” Atmosphere: The silent comedy of the immigrant Stakes: The man who cannot yet speak wants nonetheless to reach out to others

After hours of petty accusations (including the “chisel”), Lovejoy himself retorts that Plato made a similar remark about an ashtray — “Perfect mating of form and function — will you please read on, Mr. President”; later he asks Rice whether he does not give the human race too much credit for a sense of humor; Rice: “Possibly”. Atmosphere: The investigators' exasperation; the humor of Rice, who receives visitors and rumors at home every evening amid bursts of laughter Stakes: Rice's trial becomes Holt's

The foundation men ask for plans, charts, and guarantees; Rice refuses, explaining that a prior plan would kill the venture; funding is politely refused; two secretaries nonetheless offer to resign and come to work for nothing. Words: Rice: the more carefully the plans are drawn, the less there will be; impossible “above the level of bricklaying” to codify human behavior Atmosphere: politeness on both sides across a philosophical abyss Stakes: honesty versus money

A community meeting rages for hours over whether to drop Sunday lunch to relieve the kitchen staff; two camps form, as passionate as over religion or taxes; Rice sits in silence, sucking on his pipe; a compromise finally emerges: picnic supplies available, no meal served. Atmosphere: turmoil, passion out of proportion to the stakes, catharsis Stakes: the first test of community consensus, which holds despite the storm

After the students' agreement not to visit the rooms of the opposite sex, judged insufficient by the prudish members of the staff, a community meeting settles in detail the conditions for visiting in the studies; a Solomonic judgment: the sexes may mix freely so long as there are no sheets on the folding bed. Atmosphere: modesty, hard bargaining, fear of the village Stakes: the college's survival in the face of local hostility to its freedom of morals

A warm fall morning; Rice is sunning himself, Cramer nervously wonders what is expected of him; Rice opens with the question of the new world; Cramer stammers out history, then, inspired, the causes of the Depression; Rice laughs — at seeing the machinery of self-propulsion start up, or at the gap between grand designs and meager resources — and concludes: a large order. Words: Rice: “You are now entering college for the first time. What are you interested in studying?”; Cramer: “W-well, history is sort of fun”; Rice: “You've given the college a large order!” Atmosphere: Sun, the view, the student's nervousness before the founder's calm. Stakes: The birth of the autonomous student, the agent of his own education.

Rice sets out his plan to put art at the center of the curriculum; fifteen minutes of three-way conversation; Johnson announces that he has the right man — Albers —, then hesitates: there is one drawback; Rice expects the worst (blind, a cleft palate); he does not speak a word of English; Rice retorts, unfazed, that this is no drawback, they will provide interpreters; Johnson nearly falls off his chair; Rice gives him carte blanche on the spot Words: “Albers doesn't speak a word of English.” — “What's the matter with not speaking English?” Atmosphere: comic tension, a lightning decision Stakes: the founding hire

Anni, outraged by a clipping favorable to the German government, wants to throw it into the fireplace; Josef stops her: the newspaper is not hers; he slips the clipping into the advertising section of the New York Times, which is automatically thrown away Words: he tells her she has no right to destroy what is not her property Atmosphere: muted political tension in an anti-Nazi refuge Stakes: German antisemitism following the exiles right into the lobby

The students arrive with the work done during the week, or else they are refused entry; Albers, motionless in his starched smock, spreads the work out on the floor and comments on some of it at the blackboard, waving his arms; each must justify his solution and is questioned, attacked, or praised by the others; if a piece offends, he carries it to the front of the room and points out its faults with a long stick — or sends someone outside to break off a branch Words: you must see how round the jug's belly is; the ticklish life of a rose; “Only draw what you see… Style will follow” Atmosphere: Intensity, contagious energy beneath a rigid exterior; a metallic voice Stakes: Making each student see whether he is really progressing; undoing false securities

Albers places a wooden chair at the front of the room and follows its curves with his hand; he shows that some lines curve quickly while others require slowing the hand to feel their rhythm; then he sits in the chair to show that one can — or simply stands back Words: Notice how some lines curve quickly, but not all; slow the hand to feel their rhythm Atmosphere: Bodily teaching, slowed attention Stakes: Making understanding pass through the body rather than through copying

Albers hugs Yglesias in class to congratulate him on having real feelings Words: “Real feelings!” Atmosphere: Unexpected warmth from the austere man Stakes: Passion publicly defended by a restrained man

A group including at least one Black student is received; the neighbors are outraged; the community debates and votes to lodge the Black student off campus; Peggy Bailey reluctantly votes for the exclusion; her father takes it philosophically. Words: Bailey: she reluctantly voted to lodge the Black student elsewhere; neighbors: the college is the very place where free love was born. Atmosphere: shame, compromise, fear for the young college's survival Stakes: the moral price of survival in the segregated South

Looking for a head for the art department, Rice and Dreier go up to New York on Katherine Dreier's advice; Johnson shows them photos of work by Albers's students — a wire sculpture, folded-paper studies. Words: Rice, looking up: “This is the kind of thing we want”. Atmosphere: Discovery, the dazzlement of a decisive encounter Stakes: The Alberses' future and the birth of Black Mountain's art department hinge on a few photographs.

A telegram arrives from Black Mountain; then a long letter in German from Ted Dreier with the phrase “pioneering adventure”; an offer of a thousand dollars (Warburg, Mrs. Rockefeller); a reply by cable: “ja”. Words: Anni, later: “When we came across this word 'pioneering' we both said, 'This is our place.'” Atmosphere: In the depths of Berlin despair, an unhoped-for door Stakes: Emigration; a teaching project rescued across the Atlantic.

On the day the Alberses arrive, a young, buxom secretary greets them on the porch, barefoot in sandals, her pink toes on display; Anni observes and concludes that the promised freedom is real. Words: Anni, to herself: maybe this is a true story Atmosphere: first contact, a carnal, casual detail that speaks of freedom Stakes: the immigrant Alberses' gamble on this unknown place

Zastrow and Evarts translate Albers's teaching; they end up arguing over what he meant; Albers dismisses them and from then on teaches visually at the blackboard. Words: Albers: he threw them out and did it visually at the blackboard Atmosphere: linguistic misunderstanding, tension, then a sovereign decision Stakes: how to teach without a common language

After an evening of beer with the teachers, students walking home at night see a light in Albers's studio and come to bring him bottles. Atmosphere: nighttime intimacy, camaraderie between student and master Stakes: the community as family

Albers walks up the path to Lee Hall for the first time; a student asks him what he is going to teach; with his little English, he answers: “To make open the eyes”. Words: The student asks what he will teach — Albers: “To make open the eyes” Atmosphere: The arrival of an immigrant with halting English at a college newly founded in the mountains of North Carolina Stakes: The birth of the motto that will guide forty years of teaching

The students, with no chairs, work on the floor of the hall; they stop for the critiques; Albers crawls on all fours around the work to inspect it closely. Atmosphere: a large wooden room, the light of the hall, work scattered on the floor Stakes: a founding image of Albers's teaching in America: the teacher at the level of the work, in the humility of the gesture

Albers, who barely speaks English, has the students make free collages; they bring them to class; helped by two translators and then by Anni, he conveys his observations through gestures and pantomime on the way colors act on one another. Atmosphere: An informal class, small groups, nonverbal communication. Stakes: Teaching color without a common language.

The college schedule is arranged around the beginners' art classes; students, teachers, and neighbors crowd into them; a visitor describes these classes as the most dramatic and exhilarating at the college, along with Rice's. Words: A contemporary visitor: Albers's classes are “the largest and, with Rice's, the most dramatic, exciting, emotionally and intellectually satisfying, and important” Atmosphere: Intellectual and emotional exhilaration Stakes: The arts become the heart of the college's life from the first year

After a chance meeting in the street, Johnson goes up to the Alberses' for tea and asks whether they would like to go to America; they say yes without believing in it. Words: The question: would they like to go to America? The answer: yes, without expecting anything Atmosphere: Germany in 1933, uncertainty, improbable hope Stakes: The unexpected way out: six weeks later, the invitation from Black Mountain

Shortly after the closure of the Bauhaus, Johnson asks the couple whether they would like to go to America; they say yes. In New York, he learns of the founding of a college at Black Mountain with art at the center of the curriculum, whose founders want a great art teacher; he suggests Josef. Words: Anni and Josef warn Johnson that Josef does not speak English; Johnson replies that they must come anyway. Atmosphere: The urgency of exile, hope mixed with worry. Stakes: The wild gamble of an art teacher without a word of English who must found the art teaching of a new college.

On the way to visit the Blue Ridge site, Georgia stops the car and shows Rice a road sign: an extension of Columbia already bears the name they had chosen. They must find another. Atmosphere: a moment of trivial disillusionment by a summer mountain road Stakes: the name Black Mountain College born of a traffic accident

A regular stop on the fund-raising tour: on the porch, Rice and Dreier, sometimes joined by Georgia, refine their thinking on higher education; Aydelotte joins in enthusiastically; Wylie, the Englishman from the Rhodes Trust, sometimes attends Atmosphere: a summer porch, an intellectual conversation in several voices Stakes: the founding philosophy is forged far from the Blue Ridge, in the drawing rooms of the academic establishment

In the evening, Rice wants to announce the college without a plan; Dreier protests; they go to bed still arguing; Dreier stays up all night building a budget, presented at breakfast; Aydelotte concludes that he must be made treasurer. Words: Dreier: “We went to bed still debating this question. So I stayed up all night developing a budget”; Aydelotte: “Looks to me like you'd better make Ted your treasurer”. Atmosphere: a night of work, a morning of relief Stakes: The college's financial survival even before it opens

Rice spends an afternoon explaining the idea of Black Mountain to Forbes, who grudgingly likes him; Forbes pledges $5,000; as Rice leaves, Ethel decides to match the gift. Atmosphere: an island afternoon, reluctant affection Stakes: The college's founding money

A brief, neutral interview: Rice shows photos of the site, Loram makes a few comments; a polite conversation; a few days later Dreier offers her the post by telephone, to her surprise; she accepts out of a taste for adventure. Words: Loram: “It was very brief, very neutral, just polite conversation... I was quite surprised. I accepted as more of an adventure than anything else.” Atmosphere: lukewarm politeness, then surprise Stakes: Building the faculty against the grain of academic methods

Sitting before potential donors, Rice can barely hold back the urge to tell them what he thinks of their wealth. Words: Rice (thought held back): “You've got no business with all that money. Now shell out.” Atmosphere: comic tension between need and contempt Stakes: Rice, a fund-raiser in spite of himself

The mayor offers Mies two weeks' vacation during the inspection; Mies refuses and stays. The old Nazi with the gold badge arrives; a long discussion; Mies steers the visitors along the walls, diverting their attention from the central table on which lie Kandinsky's geometric analyses, which he had reluctantly kept after Kandinsky's outburst. Words: Mies to Kandinsky about his analyses: “Do we have to show these?” then “Keep it”; to the mayor: “No. I'd like to stay here. I'd like to see these people” Atmosphere: Tension, silent theatricality, a ruse of staging Stakes: Saving the school; realizing that politically it is hopeless.

Streetcar, walk, crossing the bridge: the sight of the school surrounded by the Gestapo; a run; the sentry's refusal; mentioning his status as owner opens the door; a conversation with the officer; Mies summons everyone and has everything opened for inspection; hours of searching; the hungry agents call their headquarters: “Lock it and forget it”. Words: Sentry: “Stop here.”; Mies: “This is my factory. I rented it.”; the officer: “You are the owner? Come in.” Atmosphere: Dawn, bayonets, fright (“I nearly died”), dignity under pressure Stakes: Saving the school from the accusation; proving that there is nothing to be construed

An appointment at 11 p.m.; the friends hiding in the café across the street, behind the window; an hour-long dialogue: a technical plea, a doctrinal refusal, an anathema on the name Bauhaus, Rosenberg's architectural confession (he wants a support), Mies's retort about the desk to be thrown out of the window. Words: Rosenberg: “Never!”; “my feeling demands a support”; Mies: “Don't you think the Bauhaus is a wonderful name?”; “I will see what I can do for you”; Mies: “Don't wait too long” Atmosphere: A Berlin night, a lighted café across the street, a duel of civilities between two architects Stakes: The survival of the Bauhaus negotiated between two worldviews

For three months, every other day, Mies waits on a four-inch bench designed to wear visitors out; he finally reaches the very young chief; an exchange about closing private property; the Kandinsky question; Mies's guarantee at the risk of his own arrest; the promise to speak to Goering about it. Words: Mies: “We didn't steal anything. We didn't make a revolution”; the chief: “if something happens, we pick up you” Atmosphere: An uncomfortable waiting room, stubborn patience, a strangely courteous interview Stakes: Obtaining the letter that will allow… a refusal

A call to Lilly Reich: an order for champagne despite their poverty; a meeting of the full faculty; the reading of the Gestapo's letter; general joy; then the proposal: to give thanks and announce that the faculty is closing the school itself; general delight, a toast, the end. Words: Mies: “Order champagne”; Reich: “What for? We don't have money”; the reply to the Gestapo: “Thank you very much for the permission… but the faculty has decided to close it!” Atmosphere: Ironic and solemn euphoria, victory in defeat Stakes: Turning an imposed closure into a sovereign decision; the true end of the Bauhaus, known only to those present, Albers among them

Time (June 19, 1933, “Rumpus at Rollins”) writes that Holt seems to want to be right at any cost, even at the cost of decimating his faculty. The Orlando Morning Sentinel (June 9) runs the headline “Rollins off the Gold Standard: Personality Professors Removed” about the teachers Holt had dubbed “golden personalities”. The New Republic (January 17, 1934) judges that loyalty to Holt is placed above loyalty to educational ideals, and that the case is typical of small American colleges. Time, June 19, 1933; Sentinel, June 9, 1933; New Republic, January 17, 1934

Adamic finds Rice in the midst of the crowd, laughing, asking questions, stopping to argue, discussing the mess of things, showing by his attitude that there is nothing to fear, wading into the deep mud off the path, where his voice explodes in anger as he tries to get people to stop digging in the muck and look up at the stars.

Hope Stephens heads for the door to meet a student Rice considers unworthy; he catches her and asks his question. Words: “Hope, would you want him to be the father of your children?” Atmosphere: A brusque but intimate interception amid the comings and goings of the lounge Stakes: Rice's intrusive paternal authority over the students' private lives

Rice gathers a group by the fire and makes his proposal: a religion in which the better part of oneself rises up into the body and the worst is pushed down into the surface of the world. Words: “Let's invent a religion. How about one where you get your better nature up into your body and push your worst elements down into the surface of the world?” Atmosphere: Pipe, fire, nighttime intellectual play Stakes: Rice makes every evening a classroom

On his first visit, Adamic sees Rice in the midst of the group: laughter, questions, arguments about the mess of things, then anger exploding to pull people out of the muck and turn them toward the stars. Words: Adamic: Rice “showing by his demeanor there is nothing to fear” Atmosphere: Electricity, a crowd, muck and stars Stakes: Rice's public charisma seen through an outsider's eyes
The operating budget planned for the first year, preserved in Raleigh. A total of 32,300 dollars.

Twenty-two students, fourteen of them from Rollins and only one local, Gary McGraw, admitted as a day student “by hook or crook”. Everyone lives in Lee Hall, except a few families with small children (the Dreiers in the cottages); the Rices, with their teenagers Frank and Mary, have a suite in one wing. Martin discovers his neighbor John Evarts, music critic for the Brooklyn Eagle the previous winter, consumed by doubts about his abilities. No one knows which courses will be offered or what role a formal program will play: classes wait for the community to clarify its aims. ground floor reserved for administrative offices; 2nd and 3rd floors for bedrooms; Evarts “a nice chap” who needed a shave Consequences: the community's clarification begins at once, because living does not wait

Black Mountain College opens with ten teachers and nineteen students in the YMCA complex of the Blue Ridge Assembly. 10 teachers, 19 students Consequences: Communal life at Lee Hall: shared meals and dancing after dinner on Saturday nights.

An informal opening on the vast columned porch of Robert E. Lee Hall, overlooking the Blue Ridge Mountains: no formal program, no speeches, no pomp; it ends with lunch. Joseph Martin compares the ceremony to an impromptu football game; he has forgotten any statement of educational ideals.

A few weeks before the opening, a six-page mimeographed announcement (a future small catalog) presents seven men and two women: Rice (classics and philosophy), Dreier (physics and mathematics), Georgia (chemistry), Lounsbury (government, public law, history), Loram (English and drama), Martin (English), Evarts (music), Boyden (economics), Hinckley (psychology), noting that the list will be completed. a six-page mimeographed announcement Consequences: Albers and several others arrive after the start of the fall term.

Margaret Dwight of Summit (NJ), sister of Ellsworth Dwight (three years at Rollins); Doughten Cramer of Morristown (NJ), informed by his older brother Maurice, a friend of William Aydelotte, son of the president of Swarthmore; two students from Massachusetts with no Rollins background; Frank A. Rice, who skips his last year of high school; John G. McGraw, the only nonresident student in the college's history, commuting from the town of Black Mountain; Alice Lee Swan of Oshkosh (Wisconsin), the farthest from home. 21 students, most from the East Coast; McGraw a day student

Too ill to take part, Spurr withdraws; around mid-September Georgia settles into the largest office on the ground floor of Lee Hall and posts a big “president” sign on the door, to Rice's dismay. Rice and Dreier persuade him that the title they have in mind designates an educator among his peers; Georgia holds out for “president”; Rice proposes the compromise “rector,” which will last throughout the college's history. a “president” sign; the compromise “rector” Consequences: The title of rector becomes permanent; Rice remains without an official title because of the pending AAUP report on the Rollins affair

Holt publishes a backhanded compliment: he believes Black Mountain will succeed because the college is apparently organized on the Conference Plan adopted at Rollins seven years earlier and the divisional system introduced at Rollins two years earlier; they are proud of the compliment, he says. Winter Park Reporter-Star, early September 1933, p. 1 Consequences: Reduces the founding of BMC to a copy of Rollins
